newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Clinton, Jiang expected to agree to visits.
newsitem.headline: Clinton, Jiang expected to agree to visits.

text.p: U.S. President Bill Clinton and Chinese President Jiang Zemin will probably agree to a series of high-level visits culminating in summits in Washington and Beijing when they meet on Sunday, a senior U.S. official said.

"It's likely that they will discuss and maybe announce high-level visits starting with Vice President (Al) Gore," the official told Reuters ahead of the meeting on the fringes of an Asia-Pacific summit.
Another U.S. official said: "They will unfold a series of meetings in 1997 and 1998."
This official said the likely scenario was a visit by Chinese Foreign Minister Qian Qichen to Washington in February or March, followed by a visit by Gore to Beijing in the first half of the year.
Chinese Premier Li Peng would then visit the United States followed by a Clinton-Jiang summit in Washington in the second half of 1997 after Hong Kong is transferred to Chinese rule.
Clinton, who was elected to a second four-year term on November 5, would be the first U.S. president to visit the world's most populous country since George Bush in early 1989.
Chinese-American relations began unravelling a few months later following the Tiananmen Square clampdown on dissidents in June of that year.

The Clinton-Jiang meeting on Sunday on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) conference caps a recent intensive effort to establish a new strategic basis for Chinese-American cooperation into the 21st Century. It was the fourth time the two have met.
The new approach was solidified in Beijing last week in talks between U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher and senior Chinese officials, including Jiang.
U.S. officials said Clinton planned to engage Jiang on a broad range of issues, including Asian security and China's sale of nuclear technology and missiles to Iran and Pakistan.
Trade issues and human rights were also expected to be discussed.
U.S. officials said they expected no specific progress on non-proliferation and said it was unclear whether the two leaders would make progress on trade issues.
